$schema_meta.name: EQ / PEQ / GEQ / Equalizer APO Entity Schema
$schema_meta.purpose: Machine-readable catalog of every variable used in parametric (PEQ) and graphic (GEQ) equalizer profiles, every Equalizer APO configuration feature, how these variables depend on and constrain each other, their reasoned default values, and the ideal real-world source for each value. Intended to be consumed directly by a GUI application that authors Equalizer APO config files.
primary_sources: ISO 266 preferred numbers (standard octave/third-octave center frequencies)
Harman target curve research (Olive et al., over-ear 2018 / in-ear 2019)
github.com/mirror/equalizerapo @ 53d885f7f1a097b457e17a5206b7d60f647877a8 (upstream C++ source, used to confirm LoudnessCorrection: and VSTPlugin: syntax that the SourceForge wiki does not document)
Olive, Welti, Khonsaripour et al., AES 2018/2019 (Harman over-ear/in-ear target curve research, as bundled by the AutoEQ project)
Knapp & Carter, 'The Generalized Correlation Method for Estimation of Time Delay,' IEEE Trans. ASSP, 1976 (GCC-PHAT)

Linkwitz, 'Active Crossover Networks for Noncoincident Drivers,' JAES 1976; Williams & Taylor, 'Electronic Filter Design Handbook' (Linkwitz-Riley crossover construction via squared Butterworth sections)

$schema_meta.reconciliation_note: Sections below marked with an 'implementation_status' or 'app_implementation' field were verified against a real, shipped codebase (the 'Rumble campaign', 39/39 action items closed 2026-07-10) rather than left as pure generic research. PK.description: Peaking / bell filter. Boosts or cuts a band centered on Fc. The core building block of parametric EQ.
PK.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON PK Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB Q <Q>

LP.description: Low-pass filter. Passes frequencies below Fc, attenuates above. Fixed 2nd-order (12 dB/oct) response; LPQ variant allows Q to shape the resonance at the cutoff.
LP.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON LP Fc <freq> Hz  |  ON LPQ Fc <freq> Hz Q <Q>

HP.description: High-pass filter. Passes frequencies above Fc, attenuates below. Fixed 2nd-order (12 dB/oct); HPQ allows Q control.
HP.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON HP Fc <freq> Hz  |  ON HPQ Fc <freq> Hz Q <Q>
typical_use: satellite speaker crossover (paired with subwoofer LP)
protecting small drivers from excessive excursion

BP.description: True band-pass filter (not a peaking filter). No gain parameter -- only shapes which frequencies pass through. Different from the DCX2496 hardware unit's 'BP' which is actually a peaking filter.
BP.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON BP Fc <freq> Hz Q <Q>
typical_use: isolating a narrow frequency range for diagnostic/measurement purposes

aliases: LSC (center-frequency variant with dB/oct slope param)
LS.description: Low shelf filter. Boosts/cuts everything below Fc by a constant amount. Standard LS/HS use a Q parameter to control the transition shape; LS 6dB/12dB variants use a fixed first- or second-order slope instead.
LS.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON LS Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB [Q <Q>]  |  ON LSC <slope>dB Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB  |  ON LS 6dB/12dB Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB

aliases: HSC (center-frequency variant with dB/oct slope param)
HS.description: High shelf filter. Boosts/cuts everything above Fc by a constant amount.
HS.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON HS Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB [Q <Q>]  |  ON HSC <slope>dB Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB  |  ON HS 6dB/12dB Fc <freq> Hz Gain <gain> dB
typical_use: correcting headphone treble peaks in bulk

NO.description: Notch filter -- a very narrow, deep cut at Fc, used to surgically remove a single problem frequency.
typical_use: killing a specific room mode or feedback frequency

AP.description: All-pass filter. Does not change magnitude response (no audible gain change) but shifts phase around Fc. Used for time-alignment / phase correction between drivers or channels.
AP.equalizer_apo_syntax: Filter <n>: ON AP Fc <freq> Hz Q <Q>

IIR_custom.description: Raw biquad (or higher order) filter defined directly by transfer-function coefficients. Escape hatch for filter shapes not natively supported. Sample-rate dependent -- coefficients must be recalculated whenever sample rate changes (use the If/sampleRate expression construct).
IIR_custom.caveat: Equalizer APO's own documentation advises against using this to reimplement standard biquads (PK/LP/HS etc.) because it runs slower than the native filter types.
typical_use: importing coefficients generated by external DSP design tools

GraphicEQ_band.description: A single (frequency, gain) control point in a GraphicEQ command. Unlike PK filters, a GEQ band has NO independent Q -- the shape between adjacent points is fixed by Equalizer APO as a straight line in log-frequency / linear-dB space. Effective 'sharpness' of any one band is entirely a function of how closely spaced its neighboring points are.
typical_use: importing/exporting simple EQ curves between tools

Fc_frequency.hard_constraint: Must be strictly less than Nyquist frequency (sampleRate / 2). Values approaching Nyquist can become numerically unstable in biquad form and should be soft-capped around 0.45 x sampleRate by the app's UI.
Fc_frequency.reasoned_default: No single numeric default -- should be sourced per-band from measurement or target-curve deviation. For a first manual band added by a user with no data, 1000 Hz (mid-band, least likely to cause an audible surprise) is a reasonable UI starting point.
ideal_source_priority: 1. Frequency of a measured peak/dip in the user's own room or headphone-unit response
2. Frequency flagged by a community measurement database for the exact headphone/speaker model
3. Standard GEQ band grid (ISO 266) if the profile is graphic-EQ style
4. Manual user placement via UI (least reliable, no measurement backing)
Fc_frequency.manual_vs_auto_generated: Manual vs. auto-generated range philosophy: this parameter's practical/recommended range above is the research-backed bound intended for AUTO-GENERATED content (corrections, imports, fitted curves). A real app's MANUAL/expert-editing UI is legitimately free to allow a wider hard clamp for direct human entry -- that is a deliberate, reasonable choice, not an error. What matters is that auto-generation paths are actually constrained to the tighter research bound (e.g. via an explicit clamp/cap helper applied to every auto-generated curve, with any clamping event surfaced to the user rather than silent) even when the manual UI itself is more permissive. Auto-generation grids already stay inside the research-recommended 20-20,000 Hz band by construction (their own default frequency-grid bounds), so no additional tightening was needed for Fc specifically -- only the manual UI's hard clamp is wider, and that wider ceiling only ever applies to direct human entry.

Gain.description: Boost (positive) or cut (negative) applied at/around Fc.
Gain.reasoning: Cuts are effectively 'free' (no headroom cost, no added distortion risk) and should always be preferred over boosts when correcting a peak. Boosts above +6 dB on a single band are an industry-standard caution threshold -- they demand more Preamp headroom (see Preamp entity) and increase risk of amplifier/driver strain and audible ringing at high Q.
depends_on: Preamp (every positive Gain anywhere in the chain increases the Preamp cut required)
affects: perceived loudness of the whole profile
ideal_source_priority: 1. Computed as (Target curve dB - Measured response dB) at that frequency
2. Value taken from a vetted community PEQ preset for the exact device
3. Manual user slider (creative/subjective EQ, not correction)
Gain.manual_vs_auto_generated: Manual vs. auto-generated range philosophy: this parameter's practical/recommended range above is the research-backed bound intended for AUTO-GENERATED content (corrections, imports, fitted curves). A real app's MANUAL/expert-editing UI is legitimately free to allow a wider hard clamp for direct human entry -- that is a deliberate, reasonable choice, not an error. What matters is that auto-generation paths are actually constrained to the tighter research bound (e.g. via an explicit clamp/cap helper applied to every auto-generated curve, with any clamping event surfaced to the user rather than silent) even when the manual UI itself is more permissive. Confirmed pattern: auto-generated corrections are clamped via a shared helper enforcing the default 6 dB boost cap / 12 dB cut floor, with clamping events reported through a shared summary mechanism rather than applied silently; this was extended to cover every auto-generation code path, including one (a gear-simulation delta curve) that previously had no gain bound at all.

Q.description: Controls how narrow (high Q) or wide (low Q) the filter's influence is around Fc. Q = Fc / Bandwidth(Hz).
Q.reasoning: 0.707 (1/sqrt(2)) is the Butterworth constant -- the mathematically 'neutral' choice for shelving and LP/HP filters because it produces the flattest passband with no resonant bump. For peaking/bell correction filters, most auto-EQ tools (e.g. AutoEQ) solve for Q per band rather than using one constant, but cap it (commonly around Q=6) to avoid audible ringing; a fixed default of ~1.41 is a reasonable manual-mode starting point that is neither too broad nor too surgical.
Q.conversion_formula: 1/Q = 2*sinh( (ln2/2) * BW_oct * (w0 / sin(w0)) )  where w0 = 2*pi*Fc/sampleRate  (RBJ Audio EQ Cookbook)
depends_on: Fc (bandwidth in Hz = Fc/Q, so same Q means wider Hz bandwidth at higher Fc)
affects: audible ringing risk when combined with high Gain
ideal_source_priority: 1. Solved algorithmically to best fit (Target - Measured) curve within an error tolerance (as AutoEQ does)
2. Reasoned default constant from this table, scaled by filter role (corrective vs tonal vs surgical)
Q.manual_vs_auto_generated: Manual vs. auto-generated range philosophy: this parameter's practical/recommended range above is the research-backed bound intended for AUTO-GENERATED content (corrections, imports, fitted curves). A real app's MANUAL/expert-editing UI is legitimately free to allow a wider hard clamp for direct human entry -- that is a deliberate, reasonable choice, not an error. What matters is that auto-generation paths are actually constrained to the tighter research bound (e.g. via an explicit clamp/cap helper applied to every auto-generated curve, with any clamping event surfaced to the user rather than silent) even when the manual UI itself is more permissive. No current auto-generation path produces a discrete per-band Q value at all -- every auto-generated correction is a gain-only curve (points, not discrete Q-bearing bands), so there is nothing to tighten yet. This remains an explicit open follow-up for whoever eventually builds a parametric-Q auto-generator (a fixed-Q crossover-design tool does not count, since its Q values come from a closed-form filter-design formula, not a free auto-generated fit).

Bandwidth_octaves.description: Alternative way of expressing filter width, used by the Equalizer APO 'BW Oct' filter syntax variant (matches Room EQ Wizard's FBQ2496 export format).
ideal_source_priority: Same priority chain as Q -- pick ONE representation (Q or BW) per project to avoid rounding drift from repeated conversion.
Bandwidth_octaves.manual_vs_auto_generated: Manual vs. auto-generated range philosophy: this parameter's practical/recommended range above is the research-backed bound intended for AUTO-GENERATED content (corrections, imports, fitted curves). A real app's MANUAL/expert-editing UI is legitimately free to allow a wider hard clamp for direct human entry -- that is a deliberate, reasonable choice, not an error. What matters is that auto-generation paths are actually constrained to the tighter research bound (e.g. via an explicit clamp/cap helper applied to every auto-generated curve, with any clamping event surfaced to the user rather than silent) even when the manual UI itself is more permissive. Same status as Q above -- no current auto-generation path produces a discrete bandwidth value; open follow-up, not yet applicable.

Slope_dB_per_oct.description: Roll-off steepness for shelving/cutoff filters expressed as an alternative to Q. Equalizer APO exposes this via the LSC/HSC 'x dB' variant and the fixed LS 6dB/12dB, HS 6dB/12dB filter types.
Slope_dB_per_oct.reasoning: 12 dB/oct corresponds to a standard 2nd-order (single biquad) filter -- the native resolution of nearly every Equalizer APO filter type. Steeper slopes (24/36/48 dB/oct) are achieved by cascading multiple biquads at the same Fc and increase phase shift / group delay near the corner accordingly.
Slope_dB_per_oct.convertible_to: Q (via shelf-slope parameter S in the RBJ cookbook: 1/Q = sqrt( (A + 1/A)*(1/S - 1) + 2 ) )
affects: phase shift / group delay near Fc
ideal_source_priority: Crossover design requirement (acoustic target, e.g. Linkwitz-Riley 24 dB/oct = two cascaded Q=0.707 12dB/oct stages) rather than a single universal default.

Preamp.unit: dB (must be <= 0 in virtually all real configs)
Preamp.description: A global (or per-channel) gain offset applied before/alongside the filter chain, whose entire purpose is to prevent digital clipping when the filter chain contains net positive gain anywhere in the spectrum.
Preamp.reasoned_default_formula: Preamp (dB) = -( peak positive value of the COMBINED filter magnitude response across all frequencies ) - 0.3 to 1.0 dB extra safety margin
Preamp.common_naive_shortcut: A flat -6 dB preamp is a widely used rule-of-thumb default when the combined peak hasn't been calculated, but it is NOT reliable -- large boosts (e.g. AutoEQ bass-heavy corrections) can exceed 6 dB, requiring more headroom, while a purely-cuts profile needs none at all and a blanket -6dB just wastes dynamic range/loudness.
Preamp.critical_implementation_note: The GUI app MUST calculate the actual combined frequency response of ALL active filters (they can constructively stack at overlapping frequencies) rather than naively summing each filter's own Gain value, which over- or under-estimates the true peak depending on band overlap.
affects: overall perceived loudness of the profile
ideal_source_priority: 1. Computed automatically from the combined filter response peak (see formula above)
2. Manual override by an advanced user who understands the tradeoff
3. Flat -6 dB fallback ONLY if the app cannot compute the combined response for some reason

Sample_Rate.description: The audio pipeline's operating sample rate. Not itself an EQ parameter, but every biquad coefficient and every Nyquist-adjacent Fc constraint is a function of it.
Sample_Rate.reasoning: 48 kHz is the modern Windows default output rate for most consumer audio devices. However this MUST be treated as a fallback only -- Equalizer APO exposes the live value via the 'sampleRate' expression constant and the app should read the actual device rate rather than assume one, since custom-coefficient IIR filters and Nyquist-proximity checks are wrong if the assumed rate doesn't match reality.
affects: exact biquad coefficient values for every filter
ideal_source_priority: 1. Query the live Windows audio endpoint's current format/sample rate directly
2. Read the Equalizer APO 'sampleRate' expression constant at config-generation/runtime
3. 48000 Hz as a last-resort assumption

Channel_scope.description: Which physical channel(s) a given Preamp/Filter block applies to. Set via the Channel: command; omitted = applies to all channels.
Channel_scope.important_caveat: Equalizer APO's own docs warn against scoping low-frequency filters to the LFE channel only -- most systems apply bass redirection AFTER Equalizer APO, so an LFE-only bass filter often has no effect on redirected bass. Low-frequency filters should be applied to all channels.
ideal_source_priority: User's detected speaker/headphone channel configuration (mono/stereo/quad/surround/5.1/7.1) from the Windows audio endpoint, mapped to Equalizer APO's supported Channel identifiers table.

Delay.description: Time-shifts audio on the selected channel(s). Not a frequency-domain EQ parameter but part of the same config surface -- relevant for multi-speaker/subwoofer time alignment.
Delay.reasoning: Milliseconds are preferred over samples because they give a sample-rate-independent result (Equalizer APO's own recommendation).
ideal_source_priority: 1. Measured physical/acoustic distance difference between speakers/drivers -- directly achievable via an automated mic-sweep time-alignment measurement (an exponential/Farina sweep played per channel, arrival time detected via GCC-PHAT cross-correlation, robust against room-reflection false peaks, results rebased so the earliest-arriving channel gets 0 ms since delay can only be added, never subtracted). This is no longer a purely theoretical 'ideal' -- it is a real, in-app capability distinct from a user manually measuring with a tape measure.

2. Manual user entry (e.g. from a tape-measure distance converted via distance_m / 343 * 1000, or a tooltip-provided ~1 ms per 34 cm rule of thumb) when automated measurement isn't available or practical (no measurement microphone, etc.).

graphic_eq.interpolation_rule: Equalizer APO interpolates linearly between adjacent GraphicEQ points in log-frequency / linear-dB space (a straight line on a standard log-frequency EQ graph). Outside the lowest/highest specified band, the response is flat.
graphic_eq.entity_relationship_to_peq: GEQ-to-PEQ conversion is implemented (one direction only); PEQ-to-GEQ is not implemented. The GEQ-to-PEQ method: each significant GEQ point 'owns' a log-frequency region (its own span plus half the distance to each neighbor), which is converted to a per-band Q via the standard Q/bandwidth relationship -- a directly derived relationship (denser grid produces narrower natural bandwidth), not a tuned constant. Band center frequency is the geometric mean of the owned region's edges. Because adjacent bands' skirts bleed into each other's center frequency once combined (the same way cascaded biquads stack in dB), an iterative correction pass (a bounded Newton-Raphson solve against a finite-difference Jacobian, falling back to least-squares if the Jacobian is singular) adjusts each band's gain so the final combined response matches the original GEQ curve as closely as possible. If the result must fit within a maximum band count, bands are merged (weighted-average, never silently dropped) rather than truncated. The maximum divergence between the original GEQ response and the converted PEQ response is computed and surfaced to the caller rather than assuming a perfect match. Both directions of GEQ<->PEQ conversion remain inherently lossy -- a bell-shaped peaking filter and a piecewise-linear interpolated curve cannot represent each other exactly -- this method minimizes, not eliminates, that divergence.
ideal_source_priority: ISO 266 standard grid (10/15/31 band) for interoperability with hardware/other software
Custom grid only if the app has a specific reason (e.g. matching a specific external tool's export format)

Preamp.notes: Multiple Preamp lines affecting the same channel are summed.

Filter.syntax: Filter <n>: ON <Type> Fc <freq> Hz [Gain <g> dB] [Q <q> | BW Oct <bw>]
Filter.notes: Filter number n is not interpreted by Equalizer APO and can be omitted entirely.

Filter_custom_IIR.notes: Sample-rate dependent; combine with If/sampleRate branches or inline Eval expressions to stay correct across devices.

Copy.notes: Used for channel mixing/routing, e.g. down-mixing, muting a channel, or feeding one channel's signal into another (constant values must include a decimal point to disambiguate from channel numbers).

Convolution.notes: Applies an impulse-response file (wav/flac/ogg via libsndfile). Sample rate of the IR file MUST match the device's sample rate. Linear-phase IRs cost latency equal to half the file length; minimum-phase IRs have lower but less consistent latency.

Include.notes: Loads another config file inline -- lets a profile be organized as reusable pieces (e.g. a shared Preamp/base file plus a per-headphone correction file).

Device.notes: Scopes all following commands (until the next Device command) to output/input devices whose name+connection+GUID string matches the pattern. Special pattern 'all' always matches.

Channel.notes: Scopes following Filter/Preamp commands to specific channels. Special value 'all' selects every channel.

Stage.notes: Chooses where in the Windows audio pipeline filtering happens. Default is post-mix for output devices and capture for input devices. Pre-mix is per-application (more CPU) and mainly needed for channel-count-dependent logic like upmixing.

If_ElseIf_Else_EndIf.notes: Conditionally applies blocks of config, e.g. branching on sampleRate or inputChannelCount.

Eval_and_inline_expressions.syntax: Eval: <expr>  |  inline via backticks inside another command's parameters

LoudnessCorrection.syntax: LoudnessCorrection: State (0|1) ReferenceLevel <int dB> ReferenceOffset <int dB> [Attenuation <0.0-1.0>]
LoudnessCorrection.notes: Not documented on the official SourceForge Configuration Reference wiki -- confirmed directly from Equalizer APO's own C++ source (filters/loudnessCorrection/LoudnessCorrectionFilter.cpp, VolumeController.cpp). State/ReferenceLevel/ReferenceOffset are required; Attenuation is optional (default 1.0, hard-clamped to [0.0, 1.0]). Reads live WASAPI endpoint (master, device-wide, not per-app) volume via IAudioEndpointVolume::GetMasterVolumeLevel. Applies two fixed-frequency shelf filters driven by volDiff = referenceLevel - referenceOffset - volume: a 75 Hz low shelf (Q=0.52) and a 10,000 Hz high shelf (Q=0.9), each with its own asymmetric boost/cut formula (boost side is preamp-compensated). Both shelf gains under 0.2 dB triggers a neutral/bypass shortcut. IMPORTANT: this is NOT an ISO 226 equal-loudness-contour computation -- no comment or constant in the upstream source cites ISO 226, Fletcher-Munson, or Robinson-Dadson; the 75 Hz/10 kHz corners and its numeric constants (0.55, 0.225, 0.175, 90, 100, 80) appear to be the original author's own hand-tuned heuristic, despite the superficially similar purpose to a real equal-loudness compensation curve.

VSTPlugin.notes: Not documented on the official SourceForge Configuration Reference wiki -- confirmed directly from Equalizer APO's own C++ source (filters/VSTPluginFilter.cpp, VSTPluginFilterFactory.cpp, helpers/VSTPluginLibrary.cpp). Space-separated, quote-aware key/value pairs; any key other than Library/ChunkData is treated as a named plugin float parameter. Library is required (relative paths resolve against the plugin's own default plugin-path helper; absolute paths used as-is). ChunkData and named float parameters are mutually exclusive in practice. Ordinary inline filter-chain command -- can appear per-channel/per-stage/inside an If block like any other filtering command, not a device-global plugin host. VST2 only (classic AEffect/vstPluginMain ABI) -- no native VST3 support. Plugin DLL bitness must exactly match the running APO process (32/64-bit) or it fails to load. Any failure (file not found, load failure, missing entry points, wrong architecture) logs a message and silently skips adding the filter -- it is not a hard config-parse error.

harman_over_ear_2018.description: Empirically derived preference target from Harman/Olive et al. research; widely used as the default 'neutral-preferred' correction goal for over-ear headphone EQ.
harman_over_ear_2018.use_as: target curve in (Target - Measured) EQ generation
harman_over_ear_2018.implementation_status: Implemented and cited: sourced from AutoEQ's own 'Harman over-ear 2018.csv' (118 points), resampled onto a 20 Hz-20 kHz, 12-points-per-octave log grid via log-linear interpolation. Not an abstract description -- a real, selectable, loaded target curve as of 2026-07-09.

harman_in_ear_2019.description: Companion Harman target specifically derived for IEMs, which have different coupling/leakage behavior than over-ear designs and therefore need a distinct bass/treble target.
harman_in_ear_2019.use_as: target curve in (Target - Measured) EQ generation for IEMs
harman_in_ear_2019.implementation_status: Implemented and cited: sourced from AutoEQ's own 'Harman in-ear 2019.csv', same resampling approach as the over-ear curve. Real, selectable, loaded target curve as of 2026-07-09.

diffuse_field.description: Target representing an omnidirectional, reverberant sound field; generally has less bass emphasis than Harman targets which were tuned for listener preference rather than pure measurement neutrality.
diffuse_field.use_as: target curve for studio-neutral use cases
diffuse_field.implementation_status: Implemented and cited: sourced from AutoEQ's own 'Diffuse field 5128.csv' (B&K 5128 head-and-torso-simulator variant, chosen over the GRAS KEMAR/ISO 11904-1 variants AutoEQ also bundles as the more commonly cited current rig). Real, selectable, loaded target curve as of 2026-07-09.

free_field.description: Target compensating so headphones perceptually resemble a single loudspeaker in front of the listener in an anechoic space.
free_field.use_as: target curve when trying to make headphones sound like frontal speaker playback
free_field.implementation_status: Researched, NOT implemented. No numerically-complete, freely-available free-field dataset was found during implementation -- AutoEQ's own targets/ directory publishes no free-field curve, and ISO 11904-1's free-field part is paywalled (several papers describe the curve qualitatively without publishing a full point table). Left as an explicit open follow-up rather than reconstructed/guessed, per a project convention against inventing uncited numeric constants.

iso_226_equal_loudness.description: Standardized equal-loudness-level contours (ISO 226:2003 Table 1) describing how perceived loudness varies with frequency at different absolute playback levels. Implemented: the real 29-frequency coefficient table and SPL-from-phon formula, verified against independent open-source reproductions and against the formula's own defining identity (SPL at 1 kHz equals the phon value, by definition of the phon scale). Produces a compensation curve between a calibrated reference phon/volume and the live current volume (read from the same WASAPI master-volume API Equalizer APO's own LoudnessCorrection: command uses), applied as an independent, always-recalculated layer on top of any static correction EQ -- composed before the combined-response/headroom calculation so headroom automatically accounts for it. Disabled by default; flat/no-op whenever uncalibrated or a live volume read fails.
iso_226_equal_loudness.use_as: A real, built, volume-linked loudness-compensation layer, distinct in kind from Equalizer APO's own native LoudnessCorrection: command (see equalizer_apo_commands.LoudnessCorrection) -- that command is a hand-tuned two-shelf heuristic that is NOT an ISO 226 computation despite the similar purpose; the two should not be treated as interchangeable or as documenting the same underlying math.

measurement_source_hierarchy: 1. Real measurement of the user's own physical unit/room (highest trust) -- directly actionable via a real measurement-import path (e.g. importing REW's frequency-response or Filter-Settings export formats) that can be weighted to deliberately outweigh even the best community-database tier when blended, rather than remaining a purely theoretical best case.

2. Vetted community measurement database entry for the exact model -- when multiple independent measurements of the same device exist within one provider, they can be automatically detected, averaged into a consensus curve (optionally weighted by a per-entry quality tier where the provider publishes one), and their spread displayed, rather than the app arbitrarily picking a single measurement or treating 'community database' as one undifferentiated tier.
3. Manufacturer-published frequency response spec (lowest trust -- typically smoothed and marketing-oriented, no phase/off-axis data)
4. No measurement available -- fall back to applying the chosen target curve directly with a flat assumed starting response, clearly flagged to the user as unverified

smoothing_conventions.reasoning: 1/12 octave preserves musically-relevant detail while suppressing measurement-rig noise. AutoEQ-style pipelines apply progressively heavier smoothing above roughly 6-8 kHz because measurement variance (rig/ear geometry sensitivity) increases sharply there.
smoothing_conventions.high_frequency_rule: No positive gain (boost) recommended above ~8-10 kHz -- differences in that range are dominated by measurement-rig and pinna variance rather than the actual device, so boosting risks amplifying noise/artifacts rather than a real deficiency.

biquad_cookbook.practical_implication: Every biquad coefficient set is a function of BOTH the user-facing parameters (Fc, Gain, Q/BW/Slope) AND the sample rate. The same 'Fc 100 Hz, Q 1.0' filter produces different raw coefficients at 44.1kHz vs 48kHz vs 96kHz -- Equalizer APO recalculates this internally, but any custom-IIR export must account for it explicitly.

phase_and_latency.minimum_phase_biquads: All native Equalizer APO filter types (PK/LP/HP/LS/HS/NO/AP/BP) are minimum-phase IIR designs -- near-zero added latency, some inherent phase shift concentrated around each filter's corner/center frequency. Good default for general listening, gaming, and low-latency use.
phase_and_latency.linear_phase_FIR: Achieved only via the Convolution command with a linear-phase impulse response file. Zero phase distortion but adds latency equal to half the impulse response length, and can introduce audible 'pre-ringing' on transients. Reserve for critical mastering/studio-monitoring use cases where the user explicitly accepts the latency tradeoff.
phase_and_latency.decision_rule: Default to native minimum-phase Filter/GraphicEQ commands. Only surface Convolution/linear-phase as an advanced opt-in.

cascading_and_overlap.description: When multiple bands' frequency responses overlap, their dB gains do NOT simply add arithmetically in perceived loudness, but they DO add in the underlying linear-magnitude transfer function -- meaning the true combined peak can exceed any single band's stated Gain. This is precisely why Preamp must be computed from the combined response, not from a naive per-band sum (see 'Preamp' entity).
cascading_and_overlap.cpu_and_stability: Equalizer APO explicitly recommends using its native filter types over custom IIR chains for performance; there is no hard documented cap on filter count, but practical headphone-correction profiles typically use 5-20 PK bands (per AutoEQ convention) -- beyond that, diminishing returns and increased ringing/CPU cost outweigh accuracy gains.

crossover_design.description: Linkwitz-Riley crossover construction via squared (cascaded) Butterworth sections -- LR4 (24 dB/oct) is two cascaded 2nd-order Butterworth sections at Q = 1/sqrt(2) each; LR8 (48 dB/oct) is two cascaded 4th-order Butterworth filters, each of which itself needs two sections at two different Q values, for four total stages. This is the standard method for constructing a Linkwitz-Riley filter (an order-N Butterworth response, squared) rather than a naive repeated-identical-Q cascade, which does not sum flat to 0 dB across the transition band the way a true LR crossover does.
crossover_design.q_derivation_formula: Standard analog-prototype Butterworth pole-angle formula: theta_k = (2k-1)*pi/(2*N), Q_k = 1 / (2*cos(theta_k)), for k = 1..N/2, where N is the Butterworth order corresponding to the desired LR slope (24 dB/oct -> N=2 [the trivial case, Q=1/sqrt(2)]; 48 dB/oct -> N=4). The resulting Butterworth Q list is used TWICE (each section appears twice) to build the actual LR cascade.
crossover_design.implementation_note: No new filter primitive is required to build a crossover -- Equalizer APO's native LP/HP filter types are already single 2nd-order (12 dB/oct) biquads, so an LR crossover is simply an assembly of existing filter primitives at matched Fc with the derived Q values. Optional phase alignment between the resulting high-pass and low-pass branches (e.g. against a third-party crossover that can't be edited, like a powered subwoofer's built-in low-pass) can be added via a cascade of AP (all-pass) filters at the same Fc/Q list.
sources: Linkwitz, 'Active Crossover Networks for Noncoincident Drivers,' JAES 1976

entity_relationships.note: Each filter type fixes which of Fc/Gain/Q/BW/Slope are required, optional, or not applicable.
Fc must stay below Nyquist (sampleRate/2); UI should soft-cap around 0.45x sampleRate.
Every custom biquad coefficient set is only valid for the sample rate it was computed for.
Effective bandwidth in Hz = Fc / Q; same Q value spans more Hz at higher Fc.
Use RBJ cookbook formula; pick one representation per project to avoid rounding drift.
Via shelf-slope parameter S in the RBJ cookbook.
Preamp must be at least as negative as the peak COMBINED positive gain across the spectrum, not the sum of individual band gains.
Wider/overlapping high-gain bands stack constructively, raising the true combined peak above any single band's stated Gain.
Many narrow, high-Q, high-gain bands cascaded together raise audible ringing and group-delay risk.
Corrective Gain values are ideally computed as Target curve minus Measured response at each frequency.
Defines the 'goal' shape the corrective EQ is trying to reach.
Raw measurement noise must be smoothed (1/12 oct typical) before being used to derive corrective Gain, else the EQ chases rig noise.
All filtering/level/delay commands apply only to the channels selected by the most recent Channel: command (default = all).
Everything after a Device: command applies only when the active playback/recording device matches.
pre-mix runs per-application (more CPU, sees per-app channel count); post-mix/capture run once per device (default, cheaper).
GEQ bands have no explicit Q; their real-world 'sharpness' is a side effect of how closely the surrounding points are spaced.
Delay (ms) should be computed from measured physical/acoustic distance difference, not guessed.
Equalizer APO cannot create the convolver if the IR file's sample rate differs from the live device rate.
Linear-phase IR latency = half the file length; minimum-phase IR has lower but inconsistent latency.

A speaker's summarized directivity angle (the narrower of its horizontal/vertical average) proportionally reduces how much boost an auto-generated correction is allowed to apply -- full cap above a wide-directivity threshold, damped toward half the cap at/below a narrow-directivity threshold, linearly interpolated between. Thresholds were calibrated against real measurement data showing a clean gap between well-behaved and poorly-behaved speaker directivity, not chosen arbitrarily.

entity_relationships.from: Gap between Listening-Window and Sound-Power/Early-Reflections curves
entity_relationships.note: Distinct from the proportional damping above: when a speaker's on-axis/listening-window response diverges sharply from its own local trend relative to its sound-power or early-reflections curve, that divergence signals a directivity/radiated-power artifact rather than a genuine response error worth correcting -- boosting it would raise on-axis level without fixing the underlying radiated-power problem, and can worsen off-axis sound. Correction is suppressed (toward a small residual fraction, not necessarily zero) in proportion to how far the gap exceeds its own smoothed local trend, calibrated against real measurement data showing a clean separation between well-behaved coaxial/waveguide designs and poorly-behaved crossover-lobing designs.

Device-trigger rules (matching on deviceName/connectionName) can be translated automatically into a native If/ElseIf/Else/EndIf block using the exact expression syntax already documented in equalizer_apo_commands.If_ElseIf_Else_EndIf -- exported for manual copy/paste as a complement to (not replacement for) an app-layer Include:-rewriting switching mechanism. App-trigger and time-trigger rules have no native equivalent, because Equalizer APO's expression language has no process-identity or wall-clock variable -- these are explicitly reported as untranslatable rather than silently dropped.

listener_slots.description: A per-listener hearing-correction feature (built as a redesign of an earlier parked multi-listener spec) layering an individual's own measured ear asymmetry on top of any loaded device/room-correction profile, without modifying that profile's stored data. Distinct from a 'Profile' -- a Listener Slot stores a person's hearing-test history and derived correction, not an EQ curve of its own.
listener_slots.slots: 4 fixed, nameable slots (not open-ended) -- a deliberately small, bounded set rather than a full per-user account system.
listener_slots.data_captured_per_slot: Per-slot history of hearing-threshold ('Ear Calibration') test runs, each the same per-ear-per-frequency relative-threshold + imbalance data structure the underlying test already produces. A bounded retention policy keeps only the most recent N runs per slot (oldest deleted on overflow) -- a deliberate, documented exception to a general archive-never-delete convention, justified because this is end-user runtime data, not development work product.
listener_slots.effective_correction_source: The correction actually applied is derived from the AVERAGE of a slot's saved run history (not just the most recent run), reducing the influence of any single noisy measurement session.

correction_math.principle: Weak-ear-only, capped boost -- the stronger ear is never cut.
correction_math.cap: +6 dB maximum boost per ear, matching the same boost cap already used elsewhere in the app's auto-correction pipeline (not a separately invented number).
correction_math.derivation: A per-frequency imbalance value (weaker-ear-relative-to-stronger-ear, in dB) is converted into an independent left/right correction curve: whichever ear measured weaker at a given frequency gets boosted (up to the cap) to compensate; the stronger ear is left untouched -- enforced as an invariant of the clamping step itself (a zero cut-floor), not merely an assumption about the input data.

listener_slots.render_boundary: Render-time-only composition -- the correction is NEVER written into a profile's stored data. It is composed into a profile only at the moment a config is actually rendered for preview or activation (both of the app's real render choke points), producing a new composed config object rather than mutating the stored one. When no correction is active (flat/no-op, including 'no hearing-test data for this slot'), the composition step is a zero-cost identity pass-through, so behavior is unchanged from before this feature existed.
listener_slots.interaction_with_headroom: Composition happens BEFORE the combined-response/headroom (Preamp) calculation runs, on the already-composed channel sections rather than the base ones -- so Preamp/headroom math automatically accounts for the extra correction layer. This is the same 'layer, don't merge into stored data' pattern used by the ISO 226 loudness-compensation layer, and for the same reason: both need to be included in headroom math without ever being silently baked into a saved profile's own filters.
listener_slots.session_semantics: The active listener slot resets to a configured default every app launch -- it is a session-scoped choice (like Preamp-Auto-on/off), not a value that silently persists and could surprise a different listener on next use.
listener_slots.legacy_migration: Any hearing-test history that existed before this feature shipped is copied (not moved) into the first slot on first run after upgrade, so no prior data is silently lost or duplicated on repeated migrations.
ideal_source_priority: 1. This app's own per-ear hearing-threshold test, run and saved into a listener slot
2. No correction (flat/no-op) if no listener slot is selected or has no saved test data -- this feature never guesses at a hearing profile

channel_configurations_note: The table above reflects Equalizer APO's own official, documented channel-configuration table and should be treated as the spec-level reference. A real consumer-facing app's own UI channel-layout presets are commonly a DIFFERENT, deliberately curated list (e.g. adding sub-inclusive shorthand like '2.1'/'4.1' that consumers think in, while omitting entries like bare 'Mono' or APO's specific 4-channel 'Surround' [L,R,C,RC] variant that aren't useful to a typical user) -- see app_ui_channel_presets below for a documented real-world example of this divergence, including a case where a UI shorthand preset has NO corresponding row in Equalizer APO's own official table at all.

app_ui_channel_presets.description: A real app's curated, consumer-facing channel-layout preset list, kept deliberately different from Equalizer APO's own official channel_configurations table above -- documented here as a concrete example of why the two should not be assumed to be the same list.
reconciliation_notes: 'Stereo / Headphones' and '7.1 Surround' match Equalizer APO's official table exactly.

'Surround (4.0)' uses the same channel mapping as APO's official 'Quadraphonic' entry under a friendlier name -- APO's own config literally named 'Surround' is a DIFFERENT 4-channel layout (L,R,C,RC) that this preset list does not expose at all. Worth noting explicitly so it is never mistaken for a naming bug.
'5.1 Surround' here uses the RL/RR channel identifiers (matching one of the two official 5.1 variants) rather than the SL/SR variant, kept as the more commonly recognized labeling.

'Stereo + Sub (2.1)' and 'Surround + Sub (4.1)' have NO corresponding row in Equalizer APO's own official table at all -- on hardware whose reported speaker format Equalizer APO doesn't recognize as one of its named configurations, the LFE channel identifier specifically may not resolve to any real channel, meaning a profile built from either preset could silently produce a no-op LFE filter block. A one-time user-facing warning at layout-selection time is the recommended mitigation (rather than silently switching these presets to raw numeric channel indices, which would break any other feature that pattern-matches the literal channel-name strings, such as per-ear correction logic or standard-channel-order-dependent measurement tooling).
app_ui_channel_presets.design_rationale: A curated preset list legitimately diverges from the spec's official table because it should include shorthand real users actually think in (sub-inclusive '2.1'/'4.1' counts) and can omit entries a typical consumer never needs (bare Mono, a 4-channel layout with center + rear-center but no rear-left/right). This divergence is a deliberate product decision, not an error to reconcile away -- but any preset with no official-table equivalent should be flagged to the user rather than silently assumed to work on all hardware.
